objective: By the end of this lesson you can enter, hold and level off from a constant airspeed descent, straight and turning, using only the flight instruments, and stay within ACS limits.
why: If you lose the horizon in cloud or haze, a calm, controlled descent to clear air may be your way out. Pilots without instrument training, or with rusty skills, lose control in about 10 minutes once they must rely on instruments alone [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].

warmup: In a descent with no outside view, the airspeed starts creeping up. Do you fix it with the throttle or with the nose?

key_terms.def: A descent where you hold one airspeed; the airspeed indicator tells you if your pitch is right.
The instrument that gives the most important information for pitch, bank or power at that moment.
An instrument that backs up the primary one and helps you hold it steady.
Looking at and interpreting two or more instruments, again and again, to know attitude and performance.
Staring at one instrument and ignoring the rest.
Leaving an instrument out of your cross-check.
Starting the level-off before you reach the target altitude so you don't overshoot.
Using the trim control so the airplane holds the attitude with no pressure on the controls.

body.p: The attitude indicator is the only instrument that shows pitch and bank directly and at once [[23:140|IFH 6-7]]. The altimeter, VSI and airspeed indicator show pitch indirectly [[23:137|IFH 6-4]].

While a descent is changing, the attitude indicator is the only instrument that gives a positive attitude reference. The airspeed, altimeter and VSI keep changing until the airplane settles at a steady airspeed [[23:177|IFH 7-16]].

head: Instrument
How it works
What it tells you in a descent
rows: Gyro with a vertical spin axis that stays fixed while the airplane pitches and rolls around it [[23:114|IFH 5-19]]
Nose and wing position. The little airplane's wings and dot equal about 2° of pitch [[23:114|IFH 5-19]]
Measures dynamic pressure: pitot pressure minus static pressure [[23:103|IFH 5-8]]
Primary for pitch in a constant airspeed descent [[23:211|IFH 7-50]]. Speed up = nose too low; slow down = nose too high [[23:139|IFH 6-6]]
Case vents to static through a calibrated orifice, so case pressure changes more slowly than the aneroid [[23:103|IFH 5-8]]
Rate of descent in feet per minute [[23:139|IFH 6-6]]; more sensitive than the altimeter, so it shows the trend first [[23:103|IFH 5-8]]
Sealed aneroid capsules change thickness as air pressure changes [[23:98|IFH 5-3]]
Your actual altitude, and when to start the level-off
Gyro with a horizontal spin axis [[23:114|IFH 5-19]]; not north-seeking [[23:115|IFH 5-20]]
Primary for bank in straight flight [[23:143|IFH 6-10]]
Set power to a known, predetermined value for the descent [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]

callout.text: Constant AIRSPEED descent: airspeed is primary for pitch. Constant RATE descent: VSI is primary for pitch and airspeed is primary for power [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

check.q: In a stabilized constant airspeed descent, which instrument is primary for pitch?
check.a: The airspeed indicator. Any airspeed error calls for a pitch change [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

body.p: Every instrument can mislead you. Know how each one fails so you interpret it correctly.

head: Instrument
Limitation or error
rows: Lags a few seconds behind the real change [[23:103|IFH 5-8]]. Lag grows with the speed and size of the pitch change. In turbulence, use the average of the swings [[23:139|IFH 6-6]]
Slight nose-up error in rapid acceleration, nose-down in rapid deceleration. Small bank and pitch error after a 180° turn; it corrects itself within a minute or so [[23:114|IFH 5-19]]
Drifts. Check it against the magnetic compass at least every 15 minutes [[23:115|IFH 5-20]]
Colder than standard air: you are lower than indicated [[23:100|IFH 5-5]]
Altimeter freezes, VSI reads zero, airspeed reads wrong (too low above the blockage altitude, too fast below it) [[23:98|IFH 5-3]]
Altimeter reads slightly high, airspeed reads high, VSI shows a momentary climb [[23:98|IFH 5-3]]
Errors in climbs, descents, power and airspeed changes and turbulence [[23:140|IFH 6-7]]

callout.text: If one instrument disagrees with the others, don't chase it. Cross-check the rest to find the one that is wrong.

check.q: You enter turbulence and the VSI swings between 300 and 700 fpm down. What rate are you really descending at?
check.a: About 500 fpm. Use the average of the swings, and lean on the altimeter, which is less sensitive [[23:139|IFH 6-6]].

chunks.title: Cross-check: what to look at, and when

body.p: Two basic skills make instrument flying work: cross-check and interpretation [[23:143|IFH 6-10]].

In the selected radial cross-check you spend 80 to 90 percent of the time on the attitude indicator and take quick glances out to the other instruments, always returning through the attitude indicator [[23:144|IFH 6-11]].

head: Error
What it looks like
Fix
rows: Staring at one instrument, e.g. the altimeter 200 ft low, while heading wanders [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]
Keep the eyes moving through the attitude indicator
Leaving an instrument out, e.g. not checking heading after a roll-out [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]
Use a set pattern that covers every instrument
Relying on the one instrument you understand best [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]
Confirm with at least one other instrument

callout.text: Speed up your cross-check whenever pitch, power or speed is changing, and through the whole level-off [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].

check.q: You are watching the airspeed settle during the entry and notice the heading has drifted 15°. What error is this?
check.a: Fixation on one instrument. Keep the cross-check moving through the attitude indicator [[23:146|IFH 6-13]].

body.p: Descent speeds and power settings come from your POH. Below is the IFH method [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

bullets: 1. In straight-and-level flight, slow to the descent airspeed you picked.
2. Reduce power further, to a setting you know.
3. As power comes back, lower the nose at the same time to hold the airspeed. Trim off the pressure [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].
4. Hold the heading with the heading indicator (primary bank in straight flight) [[23:143|IFH 6-10]].
5. Airspeed off? Change pitch slightly on the attitude indicator. Fast: raise the nose a little. Slow: lower it a little [[23:139|IFH 6-6]].
6. Turns while descending: combine the descent with turn technique and speed up your cross-check for both bank and pitch [[23:185|IFH 7-24]].

7. Level off early. To level off at a faster cruise speed: at 500 fpm, add cruise power 100 to 150 ft above the altitude. Hold the nose down until about 50 ft above, then smoothly raise it to level [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].
8. To level off at descent airspeed: lead by about 50 ft, raise the nose to level and add power together [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].
9. Trim, then go back to the normal straight-and-level cross-check [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

body.p: The glass-panel section of the IFH (Figure 7-66, in the first section of this lesson) uses the same idea. For a level-off to cruise speed, its lead rule is 10 percent of the descent rate: at 1,000 fpm, start 100 ft above [[23:211|IFH 7-50]].

callout.text: These limits are from ACS PA.VIII.C.S3. Aim for zero error; the limits are the most you may miss by.

check.q: You're descending at 500 fpm and want to level off at a faster cruise speed. When do you add power?
check.a: About 100 to 150 ft above the target altitude [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

chunks.title: Pitch, power and trim: small and smooth

body.p: Make pitch changes on the attitude indicator, whatever instrument told you to change [[23:140|IFH 6-7]]. Move the horizon bar no more than half a bar width at a time [[23:138|IFH 6-5]].

bullets: Correction size: aim for a VSI rate about twice the altitude error. 100 ft off = 200 fpm [[23:139|IFH 6-6]].
If the VSI shows more than 200 fpm beyond what you wanted, you are overcontrolling [[23:139|IFH 6-6]].
Use light pressure. You can't feel the controls with a tight grip [[24:367|AFH 18-18]].
Trim is correct when the airplane holds the attitude with all control pressure removed [[23:141|IFH 6-8]].
Set the attitude with the controls first, then trim. Trimming to change attitude gives erratic control [[23:143|IFH 6-10]].
Trim often and in small amounts [[23:174|IFH 7-13]].

callout.text: If you hold pressure instead of trimming, you can't tell whether a pitch change came from the airplane or from you [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].

check.q: You're 100 ft low. What VSI rate should your correction show?
check.a: About 200 fpm up, twice the error [[23:139|IFH 6-6]].

body.p: From the IFH lists of common errors in straight climbs and descents [[23:178|IFH 7-17]] [[23:180|IFH 7-19]] [[23:212|IFH 7-51]]:

head: Error
Result
Fix
rows: Small pressure, check results, wait for them
Speed up the scan on every change
Can't tell if the correction worked
Can't tell your inputs from the airplane's
Pitch on the attitude indicator; VSI only confirms
Note the descent rate and lead
Nose rises as power comes in
Hold forward pressure as power increases
Keep a fast scan until fully level

check.q: As you add power to level off, the nose pitches up and you climb past the altitude. What is this error called?
check.a: Ballooning: not holding forward pressure as power is added [[23:180|IFH 7-19]].

chunks.title: Risk: lost horizon, help, traffic and distraction

body.p: If you can't keep attitude control by the natural horizon, treat it as IMC and a real emergency [[24:366|AFH 18-17]]. First recognize it, then keep control, then get help [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].

head: Hazard
What to do
rows: Believe the instruments, not your inner ear [[24:367|AFH 18-18]]. Keep the wings level; that is the first job [[24:367|AFH 18-18]]
Loss of control in a descent

Untrained pilot: reduce power in steps of 100 rpm or 1 inch MP, descend no more than 500 fpm, nose no more than one bar width below level [[24:369|AFH 18-20]]. Avoid descending turns if you can [[24:370|AFH 18-21]]

You are in at least an urgency condition the moment you doubt position, fuel, weather or safety. Ask for help then [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]]. Squawk 7700 if needed [[34:29|AIM 6-2-2]]. Use MAYDAY or PAN-PAN, or 121.5 MHz [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]]
Not instrument rated, can't stay VFR
Tell ATC you're not instrument rated and declare a distress condition [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]]
Don't rush a maneuver. It's fine to ask the controller to slow down [[24:370|AFH 18-21]]
Treat it as a precautionary landing while you still have power and time, before it turns into a forced landing [[24:350|AFH 18-1]]

The safety pilot must hold at least a private pilot certificate with the right category and class ratings [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]], and have a good view forward and to each side, or a competent observer to help [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(2)]]. Safety pilots and CFIs tend to look inside too much [[16:15|AC 90-48E 17.2]]

Fatigue hurts attention and coordination. If you have acute fatigue, stay on the ground [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]]. Chronic stress makes performance fall off fast; a pilot under that much stress should not fly [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]]. In the air, reduce your workload and stay calm: think, weigh the options, then act [[9:21|AC 60-22 par 21e]]
Do the most important task first [[23:185|IFH 7-24]]. If you drop something, pick it up with little head movement to avoid the coriolis illusion [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]

check.q: When should you ask ATC for help?
check.a: As soon as you doubt your position, fuel, weather or safety, not after it becomes a distress [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].

scenario.title: Haze thickens over the hills
scenario.setup: You are a student on a dual practice flight at 5,500 ft. Haze thickens and the horizon disappears. Your CFI says to fly it as a real emergency: descend to 3,500 ft where it was clear earlier. You were up late last night. As you start down, your chart slides onto the floor.

questions.q: What is your first and most important job?
questions.a: Keep the wings level and fly the attitude indicator. Recognize the situation, keep control, then get help [[24:366|AFH 18-17]] [[24:367|AFH 18-18]].

questions.q: How should you set up the descent?
questions.a: Reduce power in small steps (100 rpm or 1 inch MP), keep the nose no more than one bar width below level, and keep the descent at or below 500 fpm [[24:369|AFH 18-20]].

questions.q: Should you reach down for the chart?
questions.a: Not now. Fly first. If you must pick something up, use little head movement to avoid the coriolis illusion [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].

questions.q: You are unsure what's below the haze and you're tired. Is it time to call ATC?
questions.a: Yes. Doubt about weather or safety already makes it an urgency condition. Ask for help now [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]]. Fatigue makes errors more likely [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]].

questions.q: The altimeter reads 3,800 ft and you're descending at 500 fpm. What now?
questions.a: You are 300 ft above, so get ready. To level off at a faster speed, add power at about 3,600 to 3,650 ft (100 to 150 ft lead). To level off at descent speed, start at about 3,550 ft (50 ft lead) [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

skills.do: Set descent pitch and power on an assigned heading using the cross-check and coordinated controls.
skills.practice: Under the hood with a safety pilot, slow to descent speed, then reduce power and lower the nose together, and trim [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]. Say your primary instruments out loud.

skills.do: Descend at a constant airspeed to an assigned altitude, both straight and in turns.
skills.practice: Fly straight descents, then descending turns to headings. Hold airspeed with small pitch changes [[23:139|IFH 6-6]] and speed up the scan in turns [[23:185|IFH 7-24]].

skills.do: Level off and hold altitude ±200 ft, heading ±20°, airspeed ±10 knots (ACS PA.VIII.C.S3).
skills.practice: Call out the lead point before every level-off: 50 ft at descent speed, 100 to 150 ft at 500 fpm for cruise speed [[23:178|IFH 7-17]]. Trim right after.

quiz.q: In a constant airspeed descent, which instrument is primary for pitch once you are stabilized?
quiz.why: Any deviation from the desired airspeed calls for a pitch change; the airspeed indicator is primary for pitch [[23:178|IFH 7-17]] [[23:211|IFH 7-50]].

quiz.q: During the transition into a descent, which instrument gives the only positive attitude reference?
quiz.why: The others keep changing until the airplane stabilizes [[23:177|IFH 7-16]].

quiz.q: Descending at 500 fpm, how far above the target altitude do you start adding power to level off at a faster cruise speed?
quiz.why: Lead by 100 to 150 ft at 500 fpm [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

quiz.q: To level off at descent airspeed, the lead is about:
quiz.why: Lead by about 50 ft, leveling the nose and adding power together [[23:178|IFH 7-17]].

quiz.q: You are 100 ft below your altitude. A good correction rate on the VSI is:
quiz.why: Use about twice the altitude error [[23:139|IFH 6-6]].

quiz.q: The static port freezes over in a descent. The altimeter will:
quiz.why: Trapped static pressure freezes the altimeter; the VSI reads zero [[23:98|IFH 5-3]].

quiz.q: Staring at the airspeed during the entry while heading drifts off is:
quiz.why: Fixation is staring at a single instrument [[23:146|IFH 6-13]].

quiz.q: What are the ACS limits after leveling off from a constant airspeed descent?
quiz.why: ACS PA.VIII.C.S3: altitude ±200 ft, heading ±20°, airspeed ±10 knots.

takeaways: Constant airspeed descent: airspeed is primary for pitch; fix speed with the nose.
Entry: slow to descent speed, then reduce power and lower the nose together, then trim.
Lead the level-off: about 50 ft at descent speed, 100 to 150 ft at 500 fpm for cruise speed.
Small pitch changes on the attitude indicator; trim off all pressure.
Speed up the scan on every change; avoid fixation, omission and emphasis.
Lost the horizon? Wings level, gentle descent, ask for help early.
cfi_notes: The IFH gives two level-off leads: 100-150 ft at 500 fpm (analog section, 7-17) and 10% of the descent rate (glass section, 7-50). Teach one and mention the other.

IFH Figure 7-30 is captioned 'constant airspeed descent' but labels the VSI as primary pitch and the airspeed as primary power, which matches the constant-rate text it supports. It was left out to avoid confusion.
Common student mistake: fixing a high airspeed with the throttle. In this Task, pitch controls airspeed.
Have students say the lead point out loud before each level-off; examiners watch for ballooning and overshoots.
Practice the AFH emergency version too (≤500 fpm, one bar width) so students know what to do if ever caught in IMC.
Keep your own eyes outside during hood work. AC 90-48E warns instructors and safety pilots to avoid looking inside too much.
gaps: Descent airspeed and power settings for the training airplane come from its POH; the IFH gives only the method.
The AFH has no constant-airspeed descent procedure by instruments; it points to the IFH. The step-by-step is from IFH Ch 7.
Stress is covered in general terms (PHAK 17-12, AC 60-22 par 21e); no source here gives a stress-management method specific to instrument flying.
No source gives specific guidance on emergency off-airport landings while in IMC; the AFH covers precautionary vs forced landings in general.
